newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine gov't, unions agree on two sets of talks.
newsitem.headline: Argentine gov't, unions agree on two sets of talks.

text.p: Argentina's government and the CGT labor federation agreed Thursday to hold two parallel sets of talks on labor reforms.
In one set, government officials and union leaders will meet with big industry bosses, and in the other, with small-business leaders.

President Carlos Menem's cabinet chief said at a joint news conference with CGT leader Rodolfo Daer that talks with the Group of Eight, comprising Argentina's biggest industry and commerce chambers, were set for next Thursday, February 6.
Talks with leaders of small and medium-sized businesses are slated for next Friday, February 7, Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez said.

"We share the CGT's idea of having one table for dialogue with the Group of Eight, to meet on Thursday, and another working group with all sectors of small and medium companies, which will meet Friday," Rodriguez said.
Menem's Peronist government and the CGT had cut off all dialogue after a strike on December 26 to protest at Menem's attempts to reform labor law and reduce union power by presidential decree.

The three labor decrees have since been declared unconstitutional by the courts, and Menem invited the unions back to the negotiating table to try to push through reform by consensus -- while appealing the court rulings on his decrees.
Rodriguez said the government would "analyze the suspension of the judicial process" over the decrees, though he stressed that did not mean the appeals had been dropped.

The Peronist leader argues that decentralizing collective pay talks and replacing redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance, among other reforms, are the best way to combat the country's 17.3 percent unemployment.
The CGT is traditionally an ally of the Peronists but at odds with them for the past year over austerity measures and threats to their power.
The federation has insisted the negotiations include broader economic issues such as tax evasion.

CGT chief Daer told reporters that dialogue with the government was "the only way to resolve" Argentina's economic problems. "We are not going to try to turn back the process of reform. We just want to point out its defects in issues such as tax, tariffs and finances," the union leader said.
